what_its_for: Fenofibrate is used to lower high triglycerides (a type of fat in your blood) and to raise your good cholesterol (HDL). It may also help lower your bad cholesterol (LDL). Keeping these levels in a healthy range can reduce your risk of heart disease and pancreatitis (inflammation of the pancreas).
how_to_take: Take fenofibrate exactly as your doctor tells you. Some brands must be taken WITH food to help your body absorb the medicine properly, while others can be taken with or without food — ask your pharmacist which rule applies to your specific brand. Swallow tablets or capsules whole — do not crush, chew, or break them. Try to take it at the same time every day to help you remember. Continue eating a healthy, low-fat diet while taking this medicine.
dosing: The usual dose for adults ranges from 40 mg to 160 mg once daily, depending on which brand and form you are prescribed and your specific condition. Your doctor will choose the right dose for you based on your lab results and kidney function. Always follow your doctor's prescribed dose and never adjust it on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — UNLESS it is almost time for your next scheduled dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store fenofibrate at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of the reach of children and pets. Dispose of any unused or expired medicine properly — ask your pharmacist about a medication take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid eating large amounts of fatty, greasy, or fried foods — this medicine works best when combined with a healthy diet. Limit or avoid alcohol, as it can raise your triglyceride levels and make the medicine less effective. Avoid taking antacids that contain magnesium or aluminum at the same time as fenofibrate, as they can reduce how well the medicine is absorbed. If you are also taking a statin cholesterol medicine (like simvastatin or atorvastatin), talk to your doctor, as the combination may increase the risk of muscle problems. Avoid grapefruit juice unless your doctor says it is safe.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you experience: unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, weakness, or cramping (especially with fever or dark-colored urine, which could be signs of a serious muscle problem called rhabdomyolysis); yellowing of your skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain (possible liver problems); unusual bruising or bleeding; signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, itching, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing; or severe upper stomach pain that spreads to your back (possible pancreatitis). Also call your doctor if you develop any new or worsening symptoms.
when_it_works: Fenofibrate starts working in your body right away, but you may not see results until after several weeks of treatment. Your doctor will usually check your blood lipid levels (triglycerides and cholesterol) after about 4 to 8 weeks to see how well the medicine is working. It is important to keep taking it every day even if you feel fine, because high triglycerides and cholesterol often cause no symptoms on their own.
special_populations: Older adults (65 years and older): The dose may need to be lower because kidney function naturally decreases with age. Your doctor will adjust your dose accordingly. Kidney problems: If you have kidney disease, your doctor will start you on a lower dose and monitor your kidney function regularly. This medicine may not be suitable for people with severe kidney disease. Liver problems: Fenofibrate should NOT be used if you have active liver disease or gallbladder disease. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. This medicine is generally not recommended during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Children: Safety and effectiveness in children have not been well established; use in children is uncommon.
